data.claim: The printed pid is the setsid SESSION leader (a /bin/sh -c wrapper), not the review process; a plain kill <pid> stops only the wrapper and leaves the python review running.
data.falsifier: ps shows the reported pid comm is python3 (the review itself), or SIGTERM to the reported pid makes the twin-lock review pid exit.
data.mechanism: jobs.launch() reports the pid of "setsid /bin/sh -c ... &", which is the session+process-group leader; the review (sys.executable -m ddflow) is its child/subshell grandchild, so SIGTERM to the leader does not reach it. The review lock (twin.pid) records the review own os.getpid(), so the two pids differ.
data.probe: Ran jobs.launch() in /tmp/kilo with a python command that wrote os.getpid(); printed launch() return vs the command own pid, and ps -o pid,ppid,pgid,sid,comm.
data.probe_output: launch returned pid 2298257 (sh, pgid 2298257, sid 2298257); command own pid 2298258 (python3, ppid 2298257, pgid 2298257). CONFIRMED: the printed pid is the sh session leader, the review is a separate pid (2298258).
data.question: What pid does ddflow review --detach print, and does killing it stop the review?

evidence.note: Falsifiable claim CONFIRMED by running jobs.launch() in /tmp/kilo: returned pid 2298257 was the sh session leader (pgid/sid 2298257) while the review wrote os.getpid()=2298258. Recorded as research R62b5188d3f (CONFIRMED).

Implemented in ddflow/surfaces/commands/review.py: added _detach_note(pid, log) and _detach now prints the process-group stop command (kill -- -<pid>) so the operator stops the whole detached review tree, not just the /bin/sh launcher. Regression test tests/test_review_detach.py::test_detach_note_names_a_stop_command_that_reaches_the_review fails on the unfixed code (AttributeError, no _detach_note) and passes after.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test never exercises `_detach` or a real detach. It only calls `_detach_note(2618834, "/tmp/review.log")` and asserts the string that function itself just interpolated. On the unfixed tree the failure is `AttributeError` (helper missing), not the bug: the old `c.out(f"review detached as pid {pid}...")` path is untouched, so restoring that print (or never calling `_detach_note`) still leaves this test green. It also does not show that `kill -- -2618834` reaches the python review (pid 2618836); any note containing that substring passes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_detach_note_names_a_stop_command_that_reaches_the_review

chunk_findings.detail: The prose note gained a group-kill hint, but the record passed to `c.out` is still `{"id": ..., "pid": pid, "log": log}` where `pid` is the `/bin/sh -c` session leader the bug names (2618834). A consumer that stops the review from that field (`kill` on `pid`) still signals only the wrapper and leaves the python review (2618836) running, so the next review is refused with "already being reviewed". The promised "review's own pid or a stop command" is absent from the structured output.

chunk_findings.detail: The last clause of previous finding 1 still holds: neither added test actually shows that `kill -- -2618834` reaches the still-running python review. Both tests only assert that the exact string `"kill -- -2618834"` is present in `_detach_note` output or in the dict handed to the fake `c.out`; no process group is created or signalled. The tests would still pass unchanged if the pid returned by `job_detach` were not the process group leader, or if the command string were emitted but still failed to signal the review. So the regression test does not exercise the bug's claimed mechanism, despite its name/docstring promising that the stop command "reaches the review."
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_detach_note_names_a_stop_command_that_reaches_the_review and test_detach_emits_a_stop_command_in_the_prose_and_the_data

chunk_findings.detail: `_detach_stop` prints `kill -- -{pid}` and both new tests lock that string in (`kill -- -2618834`). Pasted into bash, the builtin does not treat `--` as end-of-options: `bash -c 'kill -- -2618834'` exits with `kill: --: invalid signal specification` and sends no signal. The setsid leader (2618834) and the python review (2618836) both stay alive, so the next review is still refused with "already being reviewed". A form bash actually accepts for a process-group kill is `kill -TERM -2618834` (or `command kill -- -2618834`); the printed recipe does not stop the review on the shell operators use.
